| [THEORY-058](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-058.md) v2 | Mental disorders are maintained by self-reinforcing causal loops rather than expressing a latent common cause, which is how they can outlast their triggers | Three traditions that do not cite one another for it put self-sustaining loops where a latent cause would be. Borsboom ([LIT-547](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-547.md)) makes disorder an alternative stable state of a strongly connected symptom network, kept up by hysteresis after its trigger has gone. Salkovskis, Sighvatsson and Sigurdsson ([LIT-538](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-538.md)) make it a threat meaning protected by the behaviour it drives. Kendler ([LIT-539](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-539.md)) finds causal loops across levels, from genes to culture. The convergence is real; the evidence is indirect, simulated or clinical, and none of it is an individual time series showing hysteresis, so the account is Proposed. It says nothing about what starts a disorder. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-061](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-061.md) | In evidence-accumulation tasks, goals and instructions act on a decision by setting the parameters of the accumulation (drift, starting point or baseline, and threshold), not by specifying the response, and this holds for when to act as well as for which | Bogacz et al. ([LIT-569](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-569.md)) define cognitive control, in a two-choice task, as the adjustment of drift, starting point and threshold to maximise a utility. Ratcliff and McKoon ([LIT-576](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-576.md)) find that the manipulations behave that way: speed or accuracy instructions are fitted by boundary separation alone, stimulus proportions mainly by starting point, difficulty by drift alone. Schurger et al. ([LIT-605](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-605.md)) carry the picture to the decision of when to move: the task goal raises the baseline toward threshold and leaves the moment to fluctuation. The convergence is real; the evidence is group fits on a few paradigms, so Proposed. It does not say who sets the parameters, or how. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-074](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-074.md) | Implicit accessibility of the true self-concept is not what self-report scales of authenticity or of need satisfaction measure, though those two self-reports are not shown to be separate constructs | Schlegel, Hicks, Arndt & King (2009), [LIT-606](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-606.md): true-self accessibility, the speed of "me" judgments for traits a person takes to be her true self, correlated .05 with AI-3 authenticity and .20 with basic need satisfaction (N = 124), and each predicted meaning in life independently. The authors read this as showing the constructs differ, and concede the difference is confounded with method, reaction time against self-report. The two self-reports correlated .52, and felt autonomy was only one third of the need-satisfaction composite, whose autonomy items include "I can pretty much be myself". So the paper separates the implicit measure from both self-reports, and does not separate authenticity from autonomy. Proposed: one sample for the correlations, method unresolved. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-475](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-475.md) | In simulations from the drift-diffusion model itself, with 12 subjects and 20 to 150 trials each, hierarchical Bayesian estimation recovers every DDM parameter with less error than per-subject maximum likelihood, χ²-quantile fitting or non-hierarchical Bayes, most of all at few trials; whether the gain survives misspecification, and how much of the power gain is the hierarchy's, is not shown | Wiecki, Sofer & Frank (2013), [LIT-563](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-563.md), read in [NOTE-466](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-466.md). Experiment 1 gives the lowest trimmed recovery error for HB on every parameter, and HB beat ML on the same data sets in every condition. Experiments 2–3 report more power to detect drift differences and trial-wise covariate effects, but HB was judged by a posterior-interval test and the others by t-tests, and the clean comparison was omitted. All data were generated from DDMs, with sz = st = 0. It is the standard partial-pooling result shown for one model family, not a test of the DDM. | Active |
| [THEORY-505](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-505.md) | Questionnaire items written for morality-as-cooperation's seven domains form seven factors when rated for relevance to moral decisions, in the UK, the US and Turkey, but not when rated as agreement with moral statements, and the two formats cannot be pooled into seven domains | Curry, Jones Chesters & Van Lissa (2019), [LIT-496](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-496.md), read in [NOTE-412](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-412.md), and the independent Turkish validation by Yilmaz, Harma & Doğruyol (2021), [LIT-513](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-513.md) ([NOTE-397](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-397.md)). Relevance items fit seven factors in all three samples (CFI .98 UK, .95 Turkey). Judgement items do not (CFI .87, .83), and a seven-domain model of both fails (CFI .73, .75). The items were written from the theory and selected for fit within each domain, several subscales correlate above .8, and no item is non-cooperative. This is evidence about the instrument's structure, not about what morality contains. | Active |
| [THEORY-613](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-613.md) | The Moral Foundations Questionnaire-2's six factors, Care, Equality, Proportionality, Loyalty, Authority and Purity, fit across 19 nations, Equality and Proportionality are nearly uncorrelated in WEIRD nations, and the US split between individualizing and binding foundations appears in only three national networks | Atari, Haidt, Graham, Koleva, Stevens & Dehghani (2023), [LIT-500](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-500.md), read in [NOTE-398](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-398.md). 36 items, developed in 25 populations, fit six factors in 19 nations (ESEM CFI .979). | [THEORY-766](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-766.md) v2 | Brushing a seen rubber hand in synchrony with the hidden real hand, against asynchronous brushing, raises reports that touch is felt at the rubber hand and, more weakly and less reliably, that the rubber hand is one's own; the proprioceptive drift toward the rubber hand that accompanies these reports is not a measure of them; the standard comparison conditions do not equalise participants' expectations, so whether the stimulation or the expectation produces the report difference is open | Botvinick & Cohen (1998) and four replications read here give a synchrony effect on reports of referred touch and ownership. Rohde et al. (2011) and Abdulkarim & Ehrsson (2016) separate drift from ownership. The suggestion debate (Lush 2020; Lush et al. 2020; Ehrsson et al. 2022; Lush & Seth 2022; Roseboom & Lush 2022) shows that the standard controls do not equalise expectations. The ownership report is weaker than the referred-touch report and tracks trait suggestibility. Whether the synchronous stimulation, not expectation, produces the report difference is not settled. Promoted 2026-10-20 on the report differences measured ([ADR-047](../../../record/decisions.d/ADR-047.md) v3); the perceptual reading is [THEORY-827](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-827.md). | Active |
| [THEORY-892](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-892.md) v2 | Psychopathy as the PCL-R measures it is one dimensional construct rather than a type: its items form four correlated factors, interpersonal, affective, lifestyle and antisocial, explained by one superordinate factor, and its affective features are tied psychometrically, genetically and longitudinally to its antisocial ones, so that no one component is its essence | Hare and Neumann (2008), read in [NOTE-1094](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1094.md). The PCL-R's twenty items load on four correlated factors, which pair into Factor 1 (interpersonal, affective) and Factor 2 (lifestyle, antisocial) and are explained by one superordinate factor. The affective features are tied to the antisocial ones, so the authors deny that any component is the disorder's core, and they read the evidence as dimensional. Filed for the record's question on corporate psychopathy, which asks which of these features could be said of a corporation. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1148](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1148.md) | Single judges agree moderately on how pragmatically similar two spoken utterances are, mean pairwise correlation 0.45 to 0.72 by session, less when the utterances differ in words, so a mean over six to nine judges is much more reliable than any one judge | Ward and Marco (2024), [LIT-1812](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1812.md), read in [NOTE-1338](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1338.md) from the LREC-COLING 2024 PDF. Over 693 seed/re-enactment pairs in three sessions, mean pairwise Pearson agreement was 0.45, 0.72 and 0.66 (Table 2), and 0.80 in Session 2 when lexically different pairs were left out (p. 160). The Spearman–Brown reliability of the panel means, 0.88–0.96, is my computation. The judges talked during the session and knew each other, and all pairs are within one language, so the figure is neither a floor for a panel nor a value for translations. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1157](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1157.md) | Native-speaker crowd judges agree only modestly on the graded politeness of written requests in their own language, mean pairwise Spearman about 0.46 across nine languages, and the same bilinguals agree less on English requests, about 0.36 | Srinivasan and Choi (2022), [LIT-1799](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1799.md), read in [NOTE-1339](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1339.md) from the Findings of EMNLP 2022 PDF. The annotators had been screened for agreeing with an XLM-R classifier. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1311](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1311.md) | The BPNSFS frustration scales measure low need satisfaction in negatively keyed form, not need frustration in the sense of active thwarting, so the separation of frustration from low satisfaction in BPNSFS data, and frustration's stronger link to ill-being there, is largely a keying artefact | Murphy et al. | [THEORY-1316](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1316.md) | In eight samples pooled to 3,692 respondents, the covariance of the BPNSFS items is organized more by item keying than by need: factors sharing a keying direction correlate .64 to .75 while satisfaction and frustration of the same need correlate .17 to .38, a higher-order model grouping the six scales by keying fits better than one grouping them by need, and the frustration items carry almost no thwarting content | Murphy et al. | [THEORY-1327](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1327.md) | As Ryan and colleagues' 2022 meta-review maps it, the meta-analytic evidence for self-determination theory is concentrated in cognitive evaluation, organismic integration and basic needs theory, is mostly cross-sectional and heterogeneous, and has gaps: no meta-analysis of relationships motivation theory or of need frustration, one or two of causality orientations and goal contents, and none that separates integrated from identified regulation | Ryan, Duineveld, Di Domenico, Ryan, Steward and Bradshaw (2022), [LIT-1967](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1967.md), read in [NOTE-1500](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1500.md) from the accepted manuscript on OSF. | [THEORY-1331](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1331.md) | Deci and Ryan's General Causality Orientations Scale measures autonomy, control and impersonal orientations as three separately scored and largely independent dispositions, reliable and stable over two months, whose validity rests on correlations with self-report measures in small samples, with behaviour its weakest support | Deci and Ryan (1985), [LIT-1955](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1955.md), read in [NOTE-1531](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1531.md) from the scan on the SDT site. | [THEORY-1424](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1424.md) | Tatel finds that procedural skills with motor components decline roughly linearly with months of non-use, by about 0.06 to 0.08 standard deviations a month, losing about half of training gains within six to fifteen months, and more slowly when occasional practice occurs during the interval | Tatel (2023), [LIT-2079](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2079.md), the PhD dissertation behind Tatel & Ackerman (2025), [LIT-2088](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2088.md); read in part in [NOTE-1560](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1560.md). A random-effects meta-regression over 457 sources. The slopes are the article abstract's too; the half-loss ranges are the dissertation's (the article gives 6.5, 13 and 11 months).
